cues.text:
In a single year, one man was paid about
five hundred and fifty million

dollars. He built an empire out of the
kind of debt the rest of Wall
Street dismissed as garbage.
Then he went to prison.

Decades later, a president erased the
punishment with a stroke of a pen.
So what was Michael Milken, really?

A genius the system feared, or the face of
its greed?

There are a handful of people the world
can never quite make up its mind
about. Michael Milken is one of them.

Ask the people who admire him, and you
will hear about a misunderstood

genius. The man who pried open the doors
of capital for companies the
big banks had locked out.

Who financed jobs and growth and whole
industries that did not yet

exist. Who was then hunted down and made
an example of,

they say, for the crime of winning too
much.
Ask the people who can't stand him,
and you will hear the exact opposite.

They will tell you he is the clearest
symbol the 1980s ever produced,
a decade of greed handed a human face.

A man who bent the rules of the market
until they snapped,
paid himself more than anyone in history,

and then strolled away with a presidential
pardon and most of his
fortune still intact.
Here is the strange part.

Almost everything in both of those
portraits is true at the same time.

This is the story of how a kid from the
suburbs of Los Angeles,

working at a desk most Americans had never
heard of,

turned himself into the most powerful
financier in the country.

In one year, he was paid more than entire
corporations earned in profit.
It is the story of the idea that made him.

A simple, almost obvious insight about
debt that an entire industry had
somehow walked straight past.

It is also the story of the line he
eventually crossed,

the place where that genius curdled into
six felony counts.

And it is the story of a question that has
never really been settled.
Not by the courts, not by his money,
not even by a pardon.

Was Michael Milken a builder the system
punished for being too good at

the game? Or a criminal the system was
simply rich enough to forgive?

By the end of this, you are going to have
to decide for yourself.

To understand the man, you first have to
understand the idea,

because the idea came first, and almost
everything else grew out of it.

Picture the bond market in the early
1970s.
A bond is just a loan.

A company borrows money from investors and
promises to pay it back,
with interest, over time.
Every bond gets a grade, like a student,
from the big rating agencies.

The safe, established blue-chip companies
earn the top marks.

Investment grade. Their debt is treated
like gold,
and everyone wants to hold it.

Below a certain line sit all the other
bonds.

The debt of smaller companies, younger
companies,

companies that had stumbled once and still
carried the scar.
Below investment grade.

The market had a colder word for those.
Junk.
And the word did real damage.

Calling a company's debt junk was not just
an insult,
it was closer to a sentence.

It told every cautious investor, every
pension fund,
every bank, to stay well away.
The label became the reality.

A company branded junk could not raise
money,

and a company that cannot raise money
struggles to grow,

which makes it look even riskier than
before.
The fear fed on itself.

The rule on Wall Street was practically
carved in stone.
Respectable money does not touch junk.
It is too risky. Those companies default,
you lose your shirt, end of conversation.

So the capital that growing businesses
needed most simply was not there

for them. The door was shut, with a polite
little sign on it that said: not for you.

So the rule carried a quiet cruelty inside
it.

The biggest, safest companies, the ones
that needed help least,

could borrow all day long at the cheapest
rates in the world.

The smaller, hungrier companies, the ones
a loan might actually

transform, were left standing out in the
cold.

Money flowed toward the people who already
had it,
and away from the people who did not.
That was simply how the system worked,

and almost nobody thought to ask whether
it had to work that way.

Milken studied this same despised corner
of the market as a young man,

and he noticed something everyone else had
filed away as obvious and
never bothered to question.

He pointed to research suggesting that a
basket of these low-rated

bonds, held together as a group, actually
paid investors more than
enough to cover the handful that went bad.
Yes, some would default.

But the high interest on all the rest more
than made up the difference.

Priced for fear, the whole category was
quietly a bargain.
Sit with how large that thought is.

The entire market had agreed, without
really checking,
that junk was something to run from.

Milken's claim was that the label itself
was wrong.
That the fear was overpriced.

And that buried inside all that fear was
an enormous,

untapped opportunity, just sitting there
in plain sight.

Then he took the second step, the one that
turned a clever observation

into an empire. If these bonds were a good
deal for the people buying

them, he could do something nobody else
was willing to do.
He could help the shut-out companies,

the strivers and the upstarts the
blue-chip banks ignored,

raise real money by issuing exactly this
kind of high-yield debt.

He could open the door that had been
closed for so long.

What did that actually mean for an
ordinary company?
A cable startup, a fledgling airline,

a manufacturer with a solid plan and no
pedigree,

the kind of business a traditional bank
would wave away at the door.

Through Milken, that company could
suddenly borrow the money to build,

to hire, to grow. For the people who
believed in him,
this was the whole point.
He was not gaming the system.

He was widening it, letting in the
strivers the old club had kept out on
purpose.

He built the operation inside an
investment bank called Drexel Burnham
Lambert. Not one of the white-shoe giants.

A scrappier, second-tier firm, the kind
that had to try harder to get

noticed. In time he moved the whole
high-yield machine clear across the

country, from New York out to Beverly
Hills,

California, and ran it from a
now-legendary X-shaped trading desk,

often arriving before dawn so he would be
awake when the New York
markets opened.

That distance was its own kind of
statement.

He was not sitting at the center of the
old establishment,
waiting politely to be let in.

He was building a rival one, three
thousand miles away,

around an idea the rest of Wall Street had
been too proud,
or too frightened, to pick up.

For a good while, the idea worked the way
only the best ideas do.

Companies that could never have gotten a
loan suddenly could.
Some of them grew into giants.

The high-yield bonds Milken arranged
helped finance a wave of new

businesses that went on to reshape how
Americans lived and worked.

The door was open, and the money came
pouring through it.

If the story had stopped at that exact
moment,

Milken would be remembered as a pure
financial visionary,

a man who found money where everyone else
saw only risk.

But a tool this powerful does not stay in
one set of hands,
or get used for only one purpose.

The same machine that funded the upstarts
could fund something else
entirely. And it did.

What Milken built next went well beyond a
business.

It was closer to a kingdom, and for most
of the 1980s he sat squarely at
the center of it.

The high-yield market he had championed
exploded.

Over the decade it swelled from a
forgotten corner of finance into a

market worth well over a hundred billion
dollars,
and Milken was its undisputed king.

If you wanted to raise serious money
outside the old club,

there was one road, and it ran through
Beverly Hills, through him.

This is where the story stops being only
about plucky underdogs getting

a fair shot. Because that same flood of
money became the fuel for the
defining drama of the decade.
The corporate takeover.

In the old world, if you wanted to swallow
a giant company,
you had to already be a giant yourself.
You needed cash you simply did not have.
Milken changed the arithmetic.
He could raise vast sums of debt, fast,

and hand a relatively small player the
firepower to go after a much

larger one. The hunter no longer had to be
bigger than its prey.

It just had to be able to get Milken on
the phone.

His firm even perfected a single sheet of
paper that could put a chill
through any boardroom in America.
It was a letter stating that Drexel was,

in its own words, "highly confident" it
could raise the money for a
given takeover. Not a guarantee.
Just confidence. Yet coming from Milken,

the market treated that letter as good as
cash in hand.

A corporate raider could wave it at a
sleeping giant,

and suddenly no company in the country
felt too big to become a target.

You have to understand how that felt to
the people running America's
biggest companies.

For generations, the largest corporations
had seemed untouchable,

too vast and too expensive for anyone to
seriously threaten.

Now a far smaller rival, armed with
Milken's money,
could come for them almost overnight.

Chief executives watched their own stock
the way you watch a storm

rolling in. Milken had not just opened a
door.

He had handed out keys to the whole
neighborhood.

Once a year, the powerful and the
ambitious flew out to California to

gather around him, to raise money and
strike deals on a scale the old
Wall Street could barely picture.

For a few days, the true center of
American finance was not some marble
tower in Manhattan.

It was wherever Michael Milken happened to
be standing.

No single financier had ever loomed this
large over the American

economy. And history tends to repeat one
lesson about anyone who climbs
that high, that fast, and that visibly.

Sooner or later, the climb itself becomes
the target.

Supporters saw this as the market doing
exactly what a market is
supposed to do. Shaking the dust off lazy,
bloated companies.

Forcing complacent managers to either
perform or step aside for someone

who would. Critics saw something far
darker.

A wave of debt-fueled raids that buried
great companies under mountains

of borrowing, broke some of them apart for
scrap,
and cost ordinary people their jobs,

all to enrich a handful of financiers
standing in the middle.
They were watching the very same events.

They just could not agree on what they
were looking at.

What made the fight so bitter is that the
stakes were real on both

sides. Real companies were built with this
money,

companies that had been frozen out for
years.

And real workers found themselves on the
wrong end of a buyout,

told the factory was being sold or shut to
help pay down a mountain of

fresh debt. The same engine that created
opportunity for some created
wreckage for others.

Where a person landed on Michael Milken
often came down to which end of

that engine they happened to be standing
at.
In the middle of all of it sat the money.

Milken's personal fortune in these years
is almost hard to say out loud.

In one single year, 1987, his pay was
reported at around five hundred
and fifty million dollars.
Not his firm's haul.

His. At the time, it was the largest
annual sum anyone in America had
ever been recorded earning.
Put it in plain terms.

In a single year, one financier was paid a
sum that most successful
companies would need a decade to earn.
Not a corporation.
Not a bank. One person.

Money like that does not just buy houses
and planes.

It buys influence, access, and the benefit
of the doubt.

It also paints a very large target on your
back.

Try to actually hold that number in your
head.

By some measures, he was personally
earning more than the entire
companies he was financing.

More, in a year, than household-name
corporations booked in profit.

One man, at one desk, on the wrong coast
for Wall Street,

had turned himself into a financial
superpower.

Almost nobody outside his own operation
truly understood how it all fit
together. The web of buyers and sellers,
the favors, the timing, the financing,

lived largely inside one brilliant head
and the tight circle around it.
That was the engine of his power.

It would also, before very long, become
the source of his danger.
The more indispensable he made himself,

the more there was for someone to
investigate.

Power on that scale attracts two things at
the same moment.
Imitators, and investigators.

Wall Street had never watched anyone
gather this much control over the
flow of money this fast.

To a lot of powerful people, the rivals he
had beaten,

the executives he had cornered, the
regulators watching the takeover

wars from Washington, Milken no longer
looked like a hero flinging doors

open. He looked like a man who had simply
become too powerful,

operating inside a market only he fully
understood.

When you are the one who designed the
game,

and you are winning it by margins nobody
has ever posted before,
people stop asking how you got so good.

They start asking whether you are playing
it straight.
And in the second half of the 1980s,

the government began asking that question
out loud.

What investigators suspected was not that
Milken had backed the wrong

companies. It was that somewhere in the
blizzard of deals,

he had stopped bending the rules and
started breaking them.

Proving that would take a witness from the
inside,
someone who had sat close enough to see.

In 1986, the government found exactly
that.

Every empire seems to have a single thread
that,

once it is pulled, unravels the whole
thing.

For Milken, that thread had a name. Ivan
Boesky.

Boesky was a famous Wall Street
speculator,

an arbitrageur who made his fortune
betting on corporate takeovers,

the very deals Milken's money helped set
in motion.

In 1986, Boesky was caught in a
securities-fraud scandal of his own.

Facing his own ruin, he did what cornered
men so often do.

He cooperated. He started handing the
government other names.

And one of the names he gave them was
Michael Milken.

Boesky's cooperation pointed investigators
toward a tangle of dealings
between the two men.

Arrangements where, the government would
allege,

the true ownership of stock had been
hidden,

where favors were quietly traded, where
the disclosures the law requires
had been quietly falsified.

The genius of the open door, prosecutors
suspected,
had a hidden room tucked in behind it.

These were never going to be simple cases
to make.

The deals at the heart of them were
fiendishly complex,

layered through company after company and
account after account,

the kind of thing that took trained
investigators years just to map out.
That complexity cut both ways.

It made real wrongdoing genuinely hard to
prove.

It also made almost anything look
suspicious to outsiders who could not
follow the trail through the maze.

For two years the investigation ground
forward,

one of the largest securities-fraud probes
the country had ever

launched. Then, in 1989, it landed with
full force.

A federal grand jury handed up a
ninety-eight-count indictment against
Michael Milken.
Ninety-eight counts.

Many of them were brought under a law
called RICO,

a racketeering statute originally written
to dismantle the mafia,

now aimed squarely at a financier in
Beverly Hills.
Racketeering. Securities fraud.
Mail fraud. Insider trading.
Stock parking. Tax violations.

Prosecutors signaled they would try to
strip away well over a billion dollars.

Hold on right here, because this is the
exact spot where the headlines

blur the truth, and the difference
matters.
Those ninety-eight counts were charges.
Accusations. They were not findings,
and they were not a verdict.

The government had accused him of all of
it.

It had proven none of it, because the case
never reached a jury.

The pressure on him in that moment is hard
to overstate.

A trial under RICO could have meant
decades behind bars and the seizure
of nearly everything he owned.

A plea would cap the damage, but it would
force him to stand up in open

court and admit, out loud, that he was a
felon.

Whatever that choice was, it was not made
from a position of strength.

In April of 1990, Michael Milken made a
choice.
He chose not to fight it out at trial.
He pleaded guilty.

But the precise shape of that plea is the
thing you have to get exactly

right. He did not plead guilty to
ninety-eight counts.
He pleaded guilty to six.
Six felony counts.
Securities and reporting violations,
conspiracy, mail fraud, and a tax count,

several of them tied to those
concealed-ownership dealings with Boesky.
Now notice what is not on that list.
He did not plead guilty to racketeering.

He did not plead guilty to a standalone
charge of insider trading.

The RICO count, and the other ninety-two
counts, were dropped.
Why does that distinction still matter,
all these years later?

Because almost everyone half-remembers
this story wrong.
They picture a courtroom showdown,

a guilty verdict, a Wall Street villain
branded a racketeer and an
inside trader by a jury.
None of that happened.
There was no trial, and no verdict.
He was charged with those things, yes.

But the deal he actually made was an
admission to six specific felonies,
and racketeering was not one of them.

The towering rest of that indictment
quietly disappeared.

That gap has fueled the argument ever
since.

Critics look at the six counts and see
real crimes,

a flat admission that the king had
cheated.

His defenders look at the same six counts
and see the reverse.

Proof, they argue, that after the biggest
securities investigation in

the nation's history, with everything
imaginable on the line,

the government could only get Milken to
admit to a narrow set of
technical, regulatory offenses.

Nothing remotely like the racketeering
empire the indictment had
screamed about.
The punishment, though, was entirely real.

The financial penalty came to about six
hundred million dollars,

a record at the time, split between a fine
of two hundred million and a

four-hundred-million-dollar fund to
compensate those who had been

harmed. He was barred, for the rest of his
life,

from the securities industry he had just
spent a decade ruling.

He was sentenced to ten years in federal
prison.

Ten years. The king of Wall Street was
going to prison for a decade.

Except he wasn't. The sentence was later
cut down,

after he cooperated with prosecutors in
other cases and earned credit
for good behavior.

In the end, Michael Milken served about
two years.

To one side, two years was a slap on the
wrist,

more proof that the powerful never really
pay.

To the other, the punishment had been
crushing no matter how many months
he spent inside. A record fine.

A ruined name. Permanent exile from the
only work he had ever wanted to

do. Even his sentence, like everything
else about the man,
split the room.

So the man who had earned five hundred and
fifty million dollars in a

single year walked out of a
minimum-security prison camp in the early
1990s. Banned from his own industry.
A convicted felon.

His name welded forever to the excesses of
a decade.
The story could have ended right there,
as a tidy little morality tale.

The greedy man climbed too high, and the
greedy man fell.
It did not end there.
Because almost the moment he was free,
two things happened, one after the other,

that would scramble the verdict on Michael
Milken for the rest of his life.

The first was a death sentence of a
different kind.

Soon after his release, Milken was
diagnosed with advanced prostate
cancer. It had already spread.

The prognosis he was reportedly given was
measured not in years, but in months.

Here the story takes the turn that makes
it so genuinely hard to judge.

Faced with his own mortality, Milken threw
his fortune and his ferocious
energy straight at the disease.

He founded what became the Prostate Cancer
Foundation,

which grew into the largest private funder
of prostate cancer research

in the world. He had already created the
Milken Institute,

an economic think tank that still carries
his name.

The man the government had branded the
face of greed reinvented himself

as one of the most significant medical
philanthropists in America.

And the cancer that was supposed to kill
him inside a year?
Decades later, he is still alive.

The scale of that second act is genuinely
hard to overstate.

The same drive that had once cornered the
bond market was now aimed at

cancer research, at the scientists who
could not get funded anywhere

else. In a strange way, it was the
junk-bond insight all over again.

Find the thing the establishment has
written off,
and pour everything into it.

Only this time, the payoff was measured
not in money,
but in years of human life.
So which one is the real Michael Milken?

The felon who paid a record fine, or the
philanthropist whose money has
helped extend countless lives?

The honest answer is the uncomfortable
one.
He is both, at the same time.

And that is exactly what makes the final
chapter detonate the way it does.

Because the second thing arrived in
February of 2020.

President Donald Trump granted Michael
Milken a full pardon.

The White House statement praised his
decades of philanthropy and
described his offenses as novel.
Technical and regulatory violations,

it said, of a kind that had rarely if ever
been charged as crimes

before. It listed a long roster of
powerful people who had pushed for
the pardon. Financiers.
Media moguls. Political heavyweights.

After thirty years, the establishment had
not merely forgiven Michael

Milken. Parts of it had spent years
actively lobbying to clear his name.

By then he was no longer just a disgraced
financier.

He was a major philanthropist, a man who
convened presidents and chief

executives, whose name sat on a respected
think tank and a leading

medical charity. So the pardon did not
fall out of a clear sky.
It was the result of a long, patient,

well-funded campaign to reshape how the
world remembered him.

Whether that campaign was a search for
justice or a quiet purchase of it

is precisely the thing people cannot agree
on.

It is worth being very clear about what a
pardon is,
and what it is not.
A pardon is forgiveness.

It is the government choosing to set aside
the punishment.

What it is not is a declaration of
innocence.
It does not erase the guilty plea.

It does not say the six felonies never
happened.

Michael Milken pleaded guilty, and in the
eyes of the law,
that remains true to this day.
The pardon forgave the crime.
It did not undo it.

There was one more thing the pardon never
touched.

The lifetime ban from the securities
industry,

the regulators' judgment that he could
never again work in the business

he had transformed, stayed exactly where
it was.
Forgiven by a president.
Still barred by the regulators.

Even at the very end, the verdict on
Michael Milken came back split
right down the middle.

So you can start to see why he is a man
the world cannot settle on.

To his defenders, the pardon was simple
justice.

A long-overdue correction for a man who
had been scapegoated,
who had paid his price many times over,

and who had spent the decades since doing
extraordinary good.

To his critics, the pardon was the most
fitting ending a story about
money and power could possibly have.

Proof that in America, if you are rich
enough,

connected enough, and generous enough for
long enough,

even a record-setting financial conviction
can,
in the end, simply be wiped off the board.

Two opposite readings of the very same act
of mercy.

The unsettling thing is that neither one
of them is simply wrong.

In the end, the hardest thing about
Michael Milken is that he refuses to
fit the shape we want to force him into.

We like our financial villains to be
plainly villains,
and our geniuses to come out clean.
He is neither, and he is somehow both.

He really did see something true that an
entire market had missed,

and that insight really did open up
capital to companies that had been

locked out of it. He really did plead
guilty to six felonies,

pay a record penalty, and lose his
industry for the rest of his life.

The builder and the convict are the very
same person,

and you do not get to keep only the half
of him you happen to like.

There is a strong temptation, watching all
this,

to just pick the version that flatters
what you already believe and stop

there. The hero punished by jealous
regulators.

The crook bailed out by his powerful
friends.

But the facts are stubborn, and they
refuse to line up neatly behind
either flag.

Maybe that is the real lesson buried in
all of this.

Not a lesson about bonds, but a lesson
about us.
About how we decide, as a society,
who gets punished and who gets forgiven.

A poorer man, with a smaller fortune and
fewer powerful friends,
does not get a foundation, a comeback,
and a presidential pardon.
Milken's genius was real.

So was the machinery of wealth and
influence that,

in the end, softened nearly every
consequence the system tried to bring
down on him.

Every part of this story has two endings
stacked on top of each other.
A record fortune, and a record fine.

A ten-year sentence, and two short years
served.
A lifetime ban, and a presidential pardon.

A man told he had months to live, still
here decades later.

At every single fork, the story refuses to
hand you the clean answer you
were reaching for.

So we are going to do something we almost
never do.

We are going to leave the verdict with
you.

You have heard what he built, and you have
heard what he admitted to.
You have heard about the record fine,

the lifetime ban, the cancer, the billions
given away,

and the pardon that forgave the crime
without ever erasing it.
Genius the system punished for winning?

Or a criminal the system was rich enough
to forgive?
So tell us your verdict.

If you think you know what Michael Milken
really was,

genius, criminal, or some impossible mix
of the two,

hit like to cast your vote, and drop your
reasoning in the comments.

It is the one ruling in this whole case
that is still completely up for grabs.

Then subscribe, because next time we open
another story where the line

between brilliance and crime turns out to
be far thinner than anyone
wants to admit.
